content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all countries adopt a standardized three-test strategy for HIV testing to ensure a positive predictive value (PPV) of at least 99%, thereby minimizing false-positive diagnoses. Recent mathematical modeling has demonstrated that the WHO-recommended HIV testing strategy, combined with quality assurance measures such as retesting to confirm a positive diagnosis before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART), is cost-effective. This approach prevents misdiagnosis and avoids the unnecessary initiation of expensive lifelong treatment. Poor-quality HIV testing can result from several issues, including suboptimal test performance, improper storage or management of testing supplies, clerical or transcription errors, user errors in conducting the test or interpreting results, and inadequate documentation and record-keeping. These problems are often exacerbated by a lack of provider training, insufficient supportive supervision, or the absence of standard operating procedures. To address these challenges, quality management systems (QMS) are essential and should be expanded alongside the scale-up of HIV testing services (HTS). HIV disproportionately affects key populations, including men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, people in prisons or other closed settings, and their sexual and injecting partners. Despite increasing inclusion of these populations in national HTS guidelines, implementation remains limited, and coverage is low in most settings. Barriers to HTS uptake include HIV-related stigma and discrimination, criminalization, and punitive laws and practices. In some cases, HIV testing is misused in coercive or punitive ways against key populations, particularly in contexts where their behaviors are criminalized. Inadequate coverage and low-quality HIV services for key populations undermine national responses to HIV. Globally, men with HIV are less likely than women to know their status, be on treatment, or achieve viral suppression. In 2022, an estimated 72% of adult men with HIV (aged 15 years and older) had access to ART, compared to 82% of women in the same age group. These disparities are most pronounced in sub-Saharan Africa, where population-based surveys consistently reveal similar findings. Consequently, HIV-related morbidity and mortality rates are higher among men than women in many settings. Increasing access to testing and linkage to ART for men is critical for their health and for reducing new infections in women. Men from key populations bear a significant burden of HIV, and many remain undiagnosed. Structural barriers, including health services that are not designed to meet men’s needs, contribute to their lower uptake of health services and poorer health outcomes. Adolescents and young people are also underserved in HIV testing and care. In high HIV-burden settings, particularly in eastern and southern Africa, nearly 90% of HIV-positive adolescents (aged 10–19 years) reside. HIV burden is also high among young members of key populations, such as men who have sex with men, transgender women, young women who sell sex, and young people who use or inject drugs. In 2022, only 25% of adolescent girls and 17% of adolescent boys (aged 15–19 years) had been tested for HIV in the previous 12 months and received their results. Population-based surveys in countries like Malawi, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia suggest that only about half of young people (aged 15–24 years) with HIV are aware of their status, and only 37–46% of those aware are on treatment. Poor access to and uptake of HTS services are often due to perceived or actual poor service quality, restrictive laws and policies (e.g., age-of-consent laws), and stigma. Greater efforts are needed to improve access for adolescents, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where HIV incidence remains high among young women and girls and young members of key populations. Pregnant women with HIV, syphilis, or hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections face significant risks of mother-to-child transmission. ART is most effective in preventing HIV transmission when initiated early in pregnancy, making early testing and linkage to care critical. However, global testing coverage for syphilis and HBV in pregnant women remains significantly lower than for HIV, leading to adverse birth outcomes and congenital infections. HTS should be routinely offered as early as possible during pregnancy, and in high-burden settings, retesting may be warranted for pregnant women who initially test HIV-negative due to ongoing risk throughout the antenatal and postpartum periods. HIV testing coverage among children is often low, even in high-burden settings. Facility-based HIV testing is rarely offered routinely for children in tuberculosis (TB) and malnutrition clinics, despite high positivity rates among children tested in clinical settings. While early infant diagnosis (EID) coverage has improved in some regions, such as eastern and southern Africa, it remains very low in western and central Africa. Delays in obtaining test results and further losses in the treatment cascade result in less than one-third of perinatally infected infants being linked to services and initiated on ART in a timely manner. Barriers to HIV testing among infants and children include maternal mobility, fear of HIV disclosure, stigma, and lack of parental knowledge about the need for care. Retesting for people on ART is not recommended, as it may yield incorrect results. However, for individuals who know their HIV-positive status but have not initiated or have discontinued treatment, retesting can serve as an opportunity to re-engage in care, build trust with healthcare providers, and link to services. Testing providers should adopt a supportive, nonjudgmental approach to clients who have disengaged from care. The updated WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations on self-testing, network-based testing services, and HIV recency testing. They aim to address gaps identified in the 2019 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services and support countries in scaling up effective and efficient HTS programs. These guidelines emphasize a public health and human rights-based approach, ensuring that testing is voluntary, informed, and linked to prevention, treatment, and support services. The principles of consent, confidentiality, counseling, correct results, and connection to care (the 5 Cs) are central to all HTS efforts.
